Racing Towards History: Mika Abrahams

By: Floris Kotze | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
From Johannesburg to Formula 1 - Mika's Dream is to follow in the footsteps of F1 greats!

Unique Selling Point:
Sixteen-year-old Mika Abrahams is on the brink of history. This young talent from Johannesburg is set to become the first South African to race in Formula 1 since Jody Scheckter, the 1979 World Champion. Remarkably, he will also be the first South African of color to compete at this elite level.

Mika's journey began in the 2023 ROKiT F4 British Championship at just 14, racing with Fortec Motorsport. His impressive career includes a standout season in the Danish F4 Championship, where he secured nine podiums in 15 starts.

Mika’s passion for motorsport ignited five years ago from a simple game of F1. His determination has brought him from karting in South Africa and Italy to racing in Europe, overcoming challenges like the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2023, he joined the British F4 championship, earning notable finishes and the prestigious SA Protea national colors.

As he continues his career with Hitech GP, Mika remains dedicated to his goal: becoming an F1 champion. His rigorous training and commitment extend beyond racing, as he also coaches aspiring drivers.

Summary:
Mika Abrahams, a 16-year-old from Johannesburg, is currently competing in the British F4 championship with Hitech GP. With a background in karting and success in Danish F4, he aims to become the first South African Formula 1 driver since Jody Scheckter and the first South African of color to win in F1.

Further information:
Abrahams’ entry into F1 will also mark a significant milestone as he will be the first South African of colour to compete at this level.

Abrahams, who joined the 2023 ROKiT F4 British Championship certified by FIA at the age of 14, quickly made his mark in the racing world. Teaming up with Fortec Motorsport, he raced alongside British driver James Higgins, becoming the youngest driver on the grid from round four at Thruxton onwards.

Arriving in Britain in 2023 after four years of competitive karting in South Africa and Italy, Abrahams’ 2022 Danish F4 campaign was particularly impressive. Denmark’s F4 championship uses the first-generation Mygale chassis and allows participation from age 14. Abrahams won the third race on his debut at Sturup Raceway in Sweden and again at Jyllandsringen, achieving nine podiums in just 15 starts.

Reflecting on his journey, Abrahams shared, “My passion for motorsport ignited unexpectedly five years ago while playing an F1 game at a friend’s house. That night, I asked my dad how I could become an F1 driver. A few weeks later, I tested a kart and knew immediately that my future was in motorsport.”

Abrahams’ determination led him to Europe, where he continued to hone his skills despite the challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic. His perseverance paid off in 2021 and 2022, culminating in a stellar performance in the Danish F4 championship, where he placed third overall.

In 2023, Abrahams joined the British F4 championship with Fortec Motorsport, achieving several top-ten finishes, a pole position at Donington Park, and setting the fastest lap in race 1. His accomplishments earned him the prestigious SA Protea national colours.

Looking ahead, Abrahams continues to compete in the British F4 championship with Hitech GP, securing three podiums, including a first-place finish and two second places in 2024.

Outside of racing, Abrahams maintains a rigorous physical and mental training regimen, which includes supervised circuit training, swimming, running, and using a racing simulator for European tracks. He also dedicates time to coaching the next generation of South African drivers, offering free clinics.

“I cannot imagine my life without motorsport,” Abrahams said. “I just need someone to believe in me and see my talent and true potential. My ultimate goal is to be an F1 champion, and I am committed to making this dream a reality.”

About Mika Abrahams

Mika Abrahams is a 16-year-old racing driver from Johannesburg, South Africa, currently competing in the British F4 championship with Hitech GP. With a strong background in karting and success in the Danish F4 Championship, Abrahams aims to become the first South African Formula 1 driver since Jody Scheckter and the first South African of color to compete and win in F1.

Opening Shots of Joburg TEXT: 07:45

Abrahams House
Mika VO
My name is Mika.
I've just come back to Joburg after spending half a year in the UK.

VO1:
Mika isn’t usually a morning person, but today is different. He’s heading to one of his favourite places.

Dad:
Hey, boy. Be safe. Have fun.

Link
Hey! - How's it going? You good? - Yeah, and you? - Good to see you.
So, ordinarily, I wouldn't drive, but Mika is only in grade 11, so he doesn't have a licence.
So today, I'm driving….

Mac:
- Have you driven one of these? - Today 's my day.
- You reckon you can clap it around Zwartkops?
Mika:
Easy.
We're gonna do it.
Nice! Nice!

Link:
But, of course, here, age doesn't matter.

Mika VO:
One thing you always know is there's always a percentage that you could die when you, you know, step into that car.
But once you get in the car, you put the helmet on, you close the visor, you hear the engine start up, the revs build up, then there's just something about all of that that is so special.

VO2:
Mika Abrahams began racing at what might seem like the tender age of ten years old, but in the racing world, it's considered quite late, making his achievements even more remarkable.




Mom:
To me, he is a kind, loving, generous soul.
That's who I see first before I see a racing driver.

Dad:
I remember Mika as being this very competitive person.
Everything he needed to do, he had to be the best.
Mika went for one lap around Vereeniging.
He came out and he said, "This is what I want to do."

VO:
And so, Mika’s racing journey started with mom, Denise and Dad, Farouk Abrahams, travelling all over the country with their 10 year old son.

Mika:
So I never used to like F1.
I hated cars.
I didn't want anything to do with them.
And I went out on track and I immediately knew this was for me.
Like, you felt the speed, you felt the adrenaline, and I was like, "Yes, yes, please, give me more." And then I went out, I got out of the car, told my dad, "This is what I want to do." And then he got me a car for my birthday.
And that's how we got into karts.

VO3:
Mika excelled on the local karting tracks, but wasn;t able to escape the many risks drivers face.

Dad:
In his first year of driving, he had a very bad crash.
He got flung out of his kart.
And they had to stop the race for 20 minutes.
They had to put on one of the... Those red, right? Because of the fact that he was out of they had to secure his neck.
We went to the hospital and there's Mika lying.
And we said to Mika, "Boy, if you want to stop racing now, you're most welcome to do so." He says,

Mom:
"I cannot stop.
If you are asking me to do that, then you are not my parents." I mean, this boy just got flung out of the kart. Yes. Flung, like a rag doll. It was a very scary moment.
Yeah.

Mika:
Because my mum never likes watching me. She's like...
Mac:
Freaks out.
Mika:
Freaks out. Yeah, that's the perfect word for it. So I was kind of scared, like, "Oh, please don't cut my racing." They also felt like that's motivating for them to help me achieve my dream.

VO4:
After years of karting, Mika’s dream remained reaching Formula One - the pinnacle of motor racing. The next step was a move abroad and what’s known as Formula Four.

Vic Maharaj:
It is the pathway to Formula One. The FIA has F4, F3, F2, F1. It's very, very simple.
That's the ladder. But I wish it was that simple to actually put into practice.

VO5:
Vic Maharaj, Sporting and Services Manager at Motorsport SA understands the many challenges our racers face trying to reach the top of their sport.

Upsound from F4 Video
“He's still going to want to get to the Oh, there's a lock-up, big lock-up.
You can't race F4 in South Africa.”

Vic:
We don't have an F4 category currently. It's unaffordable in the South African landscape. So these drivers have to leave South Africa. You know, you have to win.
You have to be competitive. The only way that kids can get from Formula Four to Formula One is to try and get into a development programme with an existing F1 team.
Talent scouts are there every weekend looking, and they try to identify exceptional talent.

Upsound from F4 Video
“Mika Abraham wasn't 15 until a couple of months into this year, so joined us later on...”

Mom:
I was really nervous.I was thinking, " Can he handle this car? It's so big." And I watched him drive, and it was like a duck to water. He won on his debut race.

Mika:
When you put that helmet on, is there a beast that gets unleashed? Is there a different Mika behind there? I never want to say that for myself, but if I did have to answer that yeah, definitely.
Off-track, you try to be nice, you try to be humble, but once you step in that car, you forget about all of that, and you have to be a completely different person.

Mac:
You have to become competitive, right?
Mika:
Yeah, you need to become competitive, and that's where you let your ego just go through the roof of it in the car.
But then once you step out, it's a completely different thing.
You go back to being a good man with good values and carry your humility.

Upsound from F4 Video
“They're making them wait, and away they Abraham's on the damp part of the circuit yesterday, and once again, he's been bettered off the start by Louis Sharpe.”

Mom:
I don't watch the start of Mika's races I turn around. It's like a bit of fear, it's a bit of anxiety.
You feel like you're going to throw up, you need to go to the bathroom all at the same time.
It feels like the longest 20 minutes of your life. It's, you don't know the other drivers.
Mac:
Yeah, get out of my stance, mate.
Mom:
Exactly. He wants to drive.

Upsound from F4 Video
“But fair play, Mika Abraham, who wasn't as quick off the start as we thought, got up through the gears.”

Mika:
Like, every time I win, tears in my eyes, you know, my mum and the amount of work they put in for me just being able to have such amazing parents. So it is always a bit emotional when you get a podium and a win. You know, my dad, he's not a softie, that one, so he doesn't cry easily.
But when I see tears in his eyes, I know I did him proud. And that feeling is unmatched.

VO6:
But, just as things were falling into place for Mika, everything changed. Despite being a top contender for the British F4 title this year he quit the season and returned home, after a dispute with the team.

Mika:
Being a second year in British Formula you expect to come back and win the championship.
You know, being with one of the top you know, things didn't go to plan.
We didn't see eye to eye. And that was the hard step to take a step down from British F4 and stop this year and start preparing for next year.
VO:
The plan now is to take another step up - closer to F1.

LINK in Gym:
Even during his break, Mika cannot afford to slack off, but this isn't your average training.
This is for a racing driver.

Upsound:
“Another ten, one, two.”

Mika
I'm going to make it to F1 and that keeps me motivated.I know my dream, my goal, and I really want to achieve that badly. So I put the hours in the gym, on the sim, and I don't look at anything else. And I don't think of any plan B's, I just think of plan A.

VO7:
Mika did a few laps around Zwartkops Raceway, near Pretoria, in a Formula 1600 single-seater to give us an idea of what goes into his preparation.

Mika:
There are thousands of drivers across the world with the chance of making it to Formula 1.
And then you think to yourself, "Why am I that special one?" But then you go out and you prove to yourself why you are, and you remember why you're doing this, who you're doing it for.
It's not just for me. I want to pave the way for South African Motorsport.

Mom:
He is first person of colour to receive his South African Protea colours in single-seater racing.
He's the first African to get a double pole at Donington Park.

Mac:
And people don't even know this, right? That's the most upsetting thing about it, that nobody knows this.

Mom:
As a South African, it means just so much more, because we're people of colour, and that my son has changed history. But realistically speaking, we can only take Mika so far, and we would need support after that. Because as he gets into F3 and F2, it becomes very, very expensive, and we won't be able to do it on our own.

Mika:
Racing is like my first love.
I never want to give it up.
I still want to be 60 and driving cars around the track.
I never want to end motorsport due to a lack of funding.




Closing Link:
Having spent the last two days with Mika and his family has been nothing short of inspiring.
And it just goes to show that if you love what you do, and you do it with passion, anything is possible. I mean, from Morningside to the edge of F1, come on!

Date: 0000-00-00 Script: Opening Shots of Joburg TEXT: 07:45 Abrahams House Mika VO My name is Mika. I've just come back to Joburg after spending half a year in the UK. VO1: Mika isn’t usually a morning person, but today is different. He’s heading to one of his favourite places. Dad: Hey, boy. Be safe. Have fun. Link Hey! - How's it going? You good? - Yeah, and you? - Good to see you. So, ordinarily, I wouldn't drive, but Mika is only in grade 11, so he doesn't have a licence. So today, I'm driving…. Mac: - Have you driven one of these? - Today 's my day. - You reckon you can clap it around Zwartkops? Mika: Easy. We're gonna do it. Nice! Nice! Link: But, of course, here, age doesn't matter. Mika VO: One thing you always know is there's always a percentage that you could die when you, you know, step into that car. But once you get in the car, you put the helmet on, you close the visor, you hear the engine start up, the revs build up, then there's just something about all of that that is so special. VO2: Mika Abrahams began racing at what might seem like the tender age of ten years old, but in the racing world, it's considered quite late, making his achievements even more remarkable. Mom: To me, he is a kind, loving, generous soul. That's who I see first before I see a racing driver. Dad: I remember Mika as being this very competitive person. Everything he needed to do, he had to be the best. Mika went for one lap around Vereeniging. He came out and he said, "This is what I want to do." VO: And so, Mika’s racing journey started with mom, Denise and Dad, Farouk Abrahams, travelling all over the country with their 10 year old son. Mika: So I never used to like F1. I hated cars. I didn't want anything to do with them. And I went out on track and I immediately knew this was for me. Like, you felt the speed, you felt the adrenaline, and I was like, "Yes, yes, please, give me more." And then I went out, I got out of the car, told my dad, "This is what I want to do." And then he got me a car for my birthday. And that's how we got into karts. VO3: Mika excelled on the local karting tracks, but wasn;t able to escape the many risks drivers face. Dad: In his first year of driving, he had a very bad crash. He got flung out of his kart. And they had to stop the race for 20 minutes. They had to put on one of the... Those red, right? Because of the fact that he was out of they had to secure his neck. We went to the hospital and there's Mika lying. And we said to Mika, "Boy, if you want to stop racing now, you're most welcome to do so." He says, Mom: "I cannot stop. If you are asking me to do that, then you are not my parents." I mean, this boy just got flung out of the kart. Yes. Flung, like a rag doll. It was a very scary moment. Yeah. Mika: Because my mum never likes watching me. She's like... Mac: Freaks out. Mika: Freaks out. Yeah, that's the perfect word for it. So I was kind of scared, like, "Oh, please don't cut my racing." They also felt like that's motivating for them to help me achieve my dream. VO4: After years of karting, Mika’s dream remained reaching Formula One - the pinnacle of motor racing. The next step was a move abroad and what’s known as Formula Four. Vic Maharaj: It is the pathway to Formula One. The FIA has F4, F3, F2, F1. It's very, very simple. That's the ladder. But I wish it was that simple to actually put into practice. VO5: Vic Maharaj, Sporting and Services Manager at Motorsport SA understands the many challenges our racers face trying to reach the top of their sport. Upsound from F4 Video “He's still going to want to get to the Oh, there's a lock-up, big lock-up. You can't race F4 in South Africa.” Vic: We don't have an F4 category currently. It's unaffordable in the South African landscape. So these drivers have to leave South Africa. You know, you have to win. You have to be competitive. The only way that kids can get from Formula Four to Formula One is to try and get into a development programme with an existing F1 team. Talent scouts are there every weekend looking, and they try to identify exceptional talent. Upsound from F4 Video “Mika Abraham wasn't 15 until a couple of months into this year, so joined us later on...” Mom: I was really nervous.I was thinking, " Can he handle this car? It's so big." And I watched him drive, and it was like a duck to water. He won on his debut race. Mika: When you put that helmet on, is there a beast that gets unleashed? Is there a different Mika behind there? I never want to say that for myself, but if I did have to answer that yeah, definitely. Off-track, you try to be nice, you try to be humble, but once you step in that car, you forget about all of that, and you have to be a completely different person. Mac: You have to become competitive, right? Mika: Yeah, you need to become competitive, and that's where you let your ego just go through the roof of it in the car. But then once you step out, it's a completely different thing. You go back to being a good man with good values and carry your humility. Upsound from F4 Video “They're making them wait, and away they Abraham's on the damp part of the circuit yesterday, and once again, he's been bettered off the start by Louis Sharpe.” Mom: I don't watch the start of Mika's races I turn around. It's like a bit of fear, it's a bit of anxiety. You feel like you're going to throw up, you need to go to the bathroom all at the same time. It feels like the longest 20 minutes of your life. It's, you don't know the other drivers. Mac: Yeah, get out of my stance, mate. Mom: Exactly. He wants to drive. Upsound from F4 Video “But fair play, Mika Abraham, who wasn't as quick off the start as we thought, got up through the gears.” Mika: Like, every time I win, tears in my eyes, you know, my mum and the amount of work they put in for me just being able to have such amazing parents. So it is always a bit emotional when you get a podium and a win. You know, my dad, he's not a softie, that one, so he doesn't cry easily. But when I see tears in his eyes, I know I did him proud. And that feeling is unmatched. VO6: But, just as things were falling into place for Mika, everything changed. Despite being a top contender for the British F4 title this year he quit the season and returned home, after a dispute with the team. Mika: Being a second year in British Formula you expect to come back and win the championship. You know, being with one of the top you know, things didn't go to plan. We didn't see eye to eye. And that was the hard step to take a step down from British F4 and stop this year and start preparing for next year. VO: The plan now is to take another step up - closer to F1. LINK in Gym: Even during his break, Mika cannot afford to slack off, but this isn't your average training. This is for a racing driver. Upsound: “Another ten, one, two.” Mika I'm going to make it to F1 and that keeps me motivated.I know my dream, my goal, and I really want to achieve that badly. So I put the hours in the gym, on the sim, and I don't look at anything else. And I don't think of any plan B's, I just think of plan A. VO7: Mika did a few laps around Zwartkops Raceway, near Pretoria, in a Formula 1600 single-seater to give us an idea of what goes into his preparation. Mika: There are thousands of drivers across the world with the chance of making it to Formula 1. And then you think to yourself, "Why am I that special one?" But then you go out and you prove to yourself why you are, and you remember why you're doing this, who you're doing it for. It's not just for me. I want to pave the way for South African Motorsport. Mom: He is first person of colour to receive his South African Protea colours in single-seater racing. He's the first African to get a double pole at Donington Park. Mac: And people don't even know this, right? That's the most upsetting thing about it, that nobody knows this. Mom: As a South African, it means just so much more, because we're people of colour, and that my son has changed history. But realistically speaking, we can only take Mika so far, and we would need support after that. Because as he gets into F3 and F2, it becomes very, very expensive, and we won't be able to do it on our own. Mika: Racing is like my first love. I never want to give it up. I still want to be 60 and driving cars around the track. I never want to end motorsport due to a lack of funding. Closing Link: Having spent the last two days with Mika and his family has been nothing short of inspiring. And it just goes to show that if you love what you do, and you do it with passion, anything is possible. I mean, from Morningside to the edge of F1, come on! Suggestion 3 Viz - noise, chaos, settle on Mika’s face VO: Mika Abrahams is a rising star in South Africa. UPSOUND: VO: Already making waves in the British F4 series… Could our next F1 Champion come from Johannesburg? Mika is preparing for an event today. In fact it’s the reason we’re here. But first, there’s a short drive to reach the location. Mika Abrahams began racing at just 10 years old. It may seem young, but in the world of racing, it’s considered quite late…. Making his racing achievements even more remarkable. Mika quickly excelled on the track, leaving soccer and rugby behind. But his journey wasn’t without its challenges… The dream, of course, is to reach Formula 1. After years of karting, Mika headed abroad to start with Formula 4—the first step towards the top. Vic Maharaj, Sporting and Services Manager at Motorsport South Africa, has deep insight into the challenges our racers face on their journey to the pinnacle of the sport. Mika was tipped as one of the favorites to win the British F4 season this year - but it all came to an abrupt halt - Mika quit the season and returned home… Even though he's not currently racing, he is busy preparing for next season. Earlier, I took Mika to Zwartkops Raceway. Part of his training involved a few laps in a Formula 1600 single-seater, giving us a glimpe trackside to witness Mika’s talents first hand.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): From Johannesburg to Formula 1 - Mika's Dream is to follow in the footsteps of F1 greats!
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Sixteen-year-old Mika Abrahams is on the brink of history. This young talent from Johannesburg is set to become the first South African to race in Formula 1 since Jody Scheckter, the 1979 World Champion. Remarkably, he will also be the first South African of color to compete at this elite level. Mika's journey began in the 2023 ROKiT F4 British Championship at just 14, racing with Fortec Motorsport. His impressive career includes a standout season in the Danish F4 Championship, where he secured nine podiums in 15 starts. Mika’s passion for motorsport ignited five years ago from a simple game of F1. His determination has brought him from karting in South Africa and Italy to racing in Europe, overcoming challenges like the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2023, he joined the British F4 championship, earning notable finishes and the prestigious SA Protea national colors. As he continues his career with Hitech GP, Mika remains dedicated to his goal: becoming an F1 champion. His rigorous training and commitment extend beyond racing, as he also coaches aspiring drivers.
metadata.Summary: Mika Abrahams, a 16-year-old from Johannesburg, is currently competing in the British F4 championship with Hitech GP. With a background in karting and success in Danish F4, he aims to become the first South African Formula 1 driver since Jody Scheckter and the first South African of color to win in F1.
metadata.Further information: Abrahams’ entry into F1 will also mark a significant milestone as he will be the first South African of colour to compete at this level. Abrahams, who joined the 2023 ROKiT F4 British Championship certified by FIA at the age of 14, quickly made his mark in the racing world. Teaming up with Fortec Motorsport, he raced alongside British driver James Higgins, becoming the youngest driver on the grid from round four at Thruxton onwards. Arriving in Britain in 2023 after four years of competitive karting in South Africa and Italy, Abrahams’ 2022 Danish F4 campaign was particularly impressive. Denmark’s F4 championship uses the first-generation Mygale chassis and allows participation from age 14. Abrahams won the third race on his debut at Sturup Raceway in Sweden and again at Jyllandsringen, achieving nine podiums in just 15 starts. Reflecting on his journey, Abrahams shared, “My passion for motorsport ignited unexpectedly five years ago while playing an F1 game at a friend’s house. That night, I asked my dad how I could become an F1 driver. A few weeks later, I tested a kart and knew immediately that my future was in motorsport.” Abrahams’ determination led him to Europe, where he continued to hone his skills despite the challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic. His perseverance paid off in 2021 and 2022, culminating in a stellar performance in the Danish F4 championship, where he placed third overall. In 2023, Abrahams joined the British F4 championship with Fortec Motorsport, achieving several top-ten finishes, a pole position at Donington Park, and setting the fastest lap in race 1. His accomplishments earned him the prestigious SA Protea national colours. Looking ahead, Abrahams continues to compete in the British F4 championship with Hitech GP, securing three podiums, including a first-place finish and two second places in 2024. Outside of racing, Abrahams maintains a rigorous physical and mental training regimen, which includes supervised circuit training, swimming, running, and using a racing simulator for European tracks. He also dedicates time to coaching the next generation of South African drivers, offering free clinics. “I cannot imagine my life without motorsport,” Abrahams said. “I just need someone to believe in me and see my talent and true potential. My ultimate goal is to be an F1 champion, and I am committed to making this dream a reality.” About Mika Abrahams Mika Abrahams is a 16-year-old racing driver from Johannesburg, South Africa, currently competing in the British F4 championship with Hitech GP. With a strong background in karting and success in the Danish F4 Championship, Abrahams aims to become the first South African Formula 1 driver since Jody Scheckter and the first South African of color to compete and win in F1.
